<reason>Both sides were sharp and disciplined, but PRO (B) handled the pressure exchange more convincingly and left CON's strongest routes only partially live. CON's expiry objection was answered cleanly ("twelve months of being told versus zero days"; a sticker rise is visible for one day and nobody calls that certification), and CON simply reasserted it in closing without engaging that answer. CON's escape-hatch question was met head-on with the successor-mapping trigger and a plausible account of why the substitutes are costlier; CON's own A2 conceded shrinking is chosen because it is cheapest, which PRO turned into "the disguise is the confession." PRO's contradiction attack — the shopper is too inattentive to read a shelf flag yet attentive enough that firms retool moulds to protect her sticker — was CON's hardest problem; CON's number-versus-prose answer was coherent, but PRO's closing counter (CON's own bigger-unit-price remedy is also a number she supposedly skips, and the flag can sit inside the price line) landed last and well. CON's best surviving line — category-wide shrink plus a wide trigger produces a wall of undifferentiating notices — was genuinely strong and only partly addressed by PRO's "time to compare, trade down" framing, which keeps this competitive rather than decisive. Overall PRO's spine (CON conceded it is a price rise and never argued she shouldn't know) made the vote easier.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>PRO's B3.1/B4.5 contradiction: if the habit shopper won't read a shelf notice, why do manufacturers spend on retooling moulds to keep her sticker price unchanged? CON's A1 (she reads the number, not the prose) was a real answer, but PRO's closing turned it back — CON's own remedy relies on her reading a number too, and the flag can be placed inside the price line — leaving CON's attention argument cutting against its own alternative.</best_rebuttal>
